newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russian dissident writer Sinyavsky dead at 71.
newsitem.headline: Russian dissident writer Sinyavsky dead at 71.

text.p: Russian dissident writer Andre Sinyavsky, who spent several years in a Soviet gulag, died in a Paris suburb of cancer on Tuesday, his son said. He was 71.
"He died at home after a long illness," Iegor Sinyavsky told Reuters. "He was completing a novel."
He said his father would be buried later in the week.
Sinyavsky was arrested and tried in 1965 for writing "anti-Soviet" works, and was sentenced along with fellow writer Yuli Daniel to seven years of hard labour in Potma prison camp.
The trial is widely considered as marking the beginning of dissidence in the former Soviet Union.

After his release, Sinyavsky moved to France in 1973 with his wife Marie Rozanova and his young son, and took up a post as professor of Russian literature at the Sorbonne. He and his wife founded Sintaksis, a literary review, in 1978.
His most famous work, "Good Night", a novel loosely based on his own life, was published in 1984.

Born in Moscow on October 8, 1925, Sinyavsky fought in World War Two before writing a dissertation on Russian novelist Maxim Gorky in 1952. Assistant professor at the World Literature Institute of the Academy of Sciences, he wrote his first novel "The Circus" in 1955.
Sinyavsky published several satirical novels in France under the psudonym Abram Terts, including "The Renters" in 1959, "Lyubimov" in 1962 and a collection of essays in "Unguarded Thoughts" in 1965.

After settling in France, Sinyavsky continued to publish under his pseudonym, releasing "A Voice from the Chorus", his memoirs of the camp, in 1973, "In Gogol's Shadow" in 1975 and "Walks with Pushkin" in 1976.
In an essay which appeared in the review Continent in 1970, Sinyavsky explained his reasons for protesting against Soviet rule.

"A Russian writer who doesn't intend to write according to State's orders finds himself in the infinitely dangerous and unreal situation of an author...subject to tough measures aimed at punishing and destroying him.

"Literature has become a forbidden and perilous terrain which makes it that much more attractive, a sort of double-edged game or adventure that in itself embodies the intrigue of a fascinating novel," he wrote.

Sinyavsky's works have only been published in Russia since the early 1990s, according to his son. His last book "Ivan le Simple" (Ivan the Simple-minded), about Russian folklore, was published in France 1991.
